newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists in disarray after resignation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists in disarray after resignation.

text.p: The resignation of Bulgarian prime minister Zhan Videnov has sown fresh confusion among his ruling Socialists, who badly need a credible government to carry out economic reforms.
The new government -- Bulgaria's ninth since the end of one-party rule in 1989 -- is expected to be named by the end of the week.

One of its first tasks will be to negotiate implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund as a last resort to halt the collapse of the national currency.

After months of criticism of his handling of the economy, Videnov unexpectedly quit as premier and party leader at a party congress on December 21, wrong-footing his pro-reform critics who were unable to agree on a replacement.
"The Socialist party is really confused, but it's not ready to make any compromise," said analyst Ivan Krustev of the Centre for Liberal Strategies.
The opposition, which is no less divided than the ruling party, says the Socialists lack the popular mandate to form a new government and fresh parliamentary elections must be held.

Thousands of protesters banged pots and blew whistles outside the Socialist headquarters on Friday night as the party met to elect a new executive bureau, which excluded reformists such as U.S.-born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who had been mentioned as a possible prime minister.

Other possible candidates include the speaker of parliament, Blagovest Sendov, seen as a compromise candidate in the struggle between hardliners and reformists, and Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who emerged at the congress as a strong critic of Videnov but lacks the economic background Bulgaria's partners would like.

The trade and agriculture ministers are expected to keep their posts in the new cabinet, but Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Economic Development Roumen Gechev, and Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov may be required to take the blame for a year in which the state budget required two revisions.
Analysts say the Socialists' parliamentary allies are getting restless and the new cabinet may not last the two years remaining for the Socialists' term of office.
An opposition "salvation declaration" calling for early elections is expected to be voted by the Socialist-dominated parliament on January 10 but is certain to be defeated.
More hardship is expected with the planned implementation of the currency board, which is likely to bring more price rises and unemployment in its early stages.
The 1997 budget envisages shedding about 60,000 public sector jobs by March.
"Whoever is in charge will be pushed to follow pro-reform policies but if there is no public support, this time the crisis will come from the reforms, not the lack of them," said Krustev.

Liquidity problems among the country's poorly supervised banks last year led to 14 being placed in receivership. Loss of confidence caused a flight into dollars and the lev has crashed from 70 to the dollar to 600 in a year, a fall of more than 750 percent. Annual inflation for 1996 is estimated at 280 percent.
There is no immediate prospect that things will improve. Economists say the currency board plan and the 1997 budget draft are flawed and their chances of succeeding are slim.
Anti-communist president Zhelyu Zhelev, who leaves office on January 22, offered little hope for a brighter 1997 in his New Year's address to the nation.

"1996 is probably the hardest year as the Bulgarian people lost their hope for a better future," he said, offering an ironic apology on behalf of politicians for the nation's economic and social woes. "I feel ashamed that the Bulgarian state has been driven to this miserable situation."
